title: Navigation Without a Compass
content:
If you must move, you can hold a rough direction without a compass using the sun, stars, and terrain.

Sun:
- It rises in the east and sets in the west everywhere. That alone fixes an approximate east-west line at dawn and dusk.
- Shadow-stick method: push a stick upright in level ground. Mark the tip of its shadow. Wait 15-20 minutes and mark the new tip. The first mark is roughly west, the second roughly east; the line between them runs east-west, and perpendicular gives north-south.

Stars (Northern Hemisphere):
- Find the North Star (Polaris). Locate the Big Dipper; the two stars at the end of its 'cup' point to Polaris. Polaris sits due north and barely moves through the night.

Stars (Southern Hemisphere):
- Use the Southern Cross. Extend the long axis of the cross about 4.5 times its length to a point in the sky; straight down from there is roughly south.

General practice:
- Pick a distant landmark in your chosen direction, walk to it, then pick another. This keeps you from circling.
- Note your back-trail and obvious features so you can retrace your steps. When in doubt in a true emergency, conserving energy and signaling usually beats wandering.
